question.text: What is the trace in the $yz$-plane of the hyperbolic cylinder $\dfrac {(x-4)^2} 2 - \dfrac {(y+1)^2}7 = 1?$
question.explanation:
To find the trace in the $yz$-plane, we substitute $x=0$ into the equation of the cylinder, and simplify:

\begin{align*} \dfrac {(0-4)^2} 2 - \dfrac {(y+1)^2}7 &= 1 \\[5pt] 8 - \dfrac {(y+1)^2}7 &= 1 \\[5pt] \dfrac{(y+1)^2}{7} &= 7 \\[5pt] (y+1)^2 &= 49 \\[5pt] y+1 & = \pm 7 \\[5pt] y &= -1 \pm 7 \\[5pt] y& = -8, 6 \end{align*}

This gives us the equation of two lines $y=-8$ and $y=6$ in the $yz$-plane.

question.text: What is the trace in the $xz$-plane of the elliptic cylinder $\dfrac {(x-4)^2} 8 + \dfrac {(y-1)^2}2 = 1?$
question.explanation:
To find the trace in the $xz$-plane, we substitute $y=0$ into the equation of the cylinder, and simplify:

\begin{align*} \dfrac {(x-4)^2} 8 + \dfrac {(0-1)^2}2 &= 1 \\[5pt] \dfrac {(x-4)^2} 8 + \dfrac{1}{2} & = 1 \\[5pt] \dfrac {(x-4)^2} 8 &= \dfrac{1}{2} \\[5pt] (x-4)^2 &=4 \\[5pt] x-4 &= \pm 2\\[5pt] x &= 4 \pm 2 \\[5pt] x& = 2, 6 \end{align*}

This gives us the equation of two lines $x=2$ and $x= 6$ in the $xz$-plane.

question.text: What is the domain in the $xy$-plane of the hyperbolic cylinder $\dfrac{x^2}{3} - \dfrac{(y+1)^2}{4} = 1?$
question.explanation:
The full expression describing all points on our hyperbolic cylinder is \[ \dfrac{x^2}{3} - \dfrac{(y+1)^2}{4} = 1, \qquad z=k \] where $k\in\mathbb R$ can vary arbitrarily.

The domain of any cylinder in the $xy$-plane is its base curve. Hence, in this case, the domain is \[ \left\{ (x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 :\ \dfrac{x^2}{3} - \dfrac{(y+1)^2}{4} = 1 \right\}. \]

This is a hyperbola centered at $(0,-1).$

question.text: What is the domain in the $xy$-plane of the parabolic cylinder $(x-1)^2 = 3y?$
question.choice1: An upward-opening parabola with a vertex at $(1,0)$
question.choice2: An upward-opening parabola with a vertex at $(-1,0)$
question.choice3: A rightward-opening parabola with a vertex at $(1,0)$
question.choice4: A rightward-opening parabola with a vertex at $(-1,0)$
